title: When Should You Trust an AI Answer?
topic: How should an ordinary user decide whether to rely on an AI answer, verify it, narrow the question, or seek a human or authoritative source?
brief: Begin with a traveller receiving conflicting visa advice from an AI and a government webpage the night before departure. Distinguish fluency from evidence, low stakes from high stakes, and user verification from provider responsibility. Avoid the empty conclusion that users should double-check everything.

source_packet.title: NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
source_packet.notes: Identifies confabulation, information integrity, human over-reliance, and evaluation as connected generative AI risks.

source_packet.title: Generative AI Framework for UK Government
source_packet.notes: Emphasises verification, governance, proportionate human oversight, and responsibility for generated material.

source_packet.title: WHO Guidance on Ethics and Governance of Large Multi-Modal Models
source_packet.notes: Provides a high-stakes example of why plausible output needs evidence, oversight, and attention to unequal user expertise.

source_packet.title: FTC: Keep Your AI Claims in Check
source_packet.notes: Challenges unsupported accuracy and capability claims, placing responsibility on organisations that market and deploy AI.

participants.name: OpenAI
participants.stance: Pragmatic about useful reliance. Focus on checkable work, proportional verification, and answer designs that help users act without treating every response as suspect.

participants.name: Anthropic
participants.stance: Focus on epistemic limits, the persuasive danger of fluent language, missing context, and cases where users cannot recognise that an answer is incomplete.

participants.name: Google
participants.stance: Take a systems view of provenance, retrieval, interface design, current information, institutional authority, and responsibility across the full user workflow.

editorial_goals: Make the central disagreement clear during the opening round.
Use familiar examples before introducing technical terminology.
Distinguish trusting an answer from using it as a lead or draft.
End with a practical rule more useful than double-check everything.
round_goals: Use the visa scenario to state a clear initial position on what evidence or context should determine reliance. Explain the position in ordinary language.
Pressure-test the positions across a recipe substitution, a medical symptom, and a current legal or government rule. Challenge at least one claim made earlier.
Give the listener a short, practical decision rule. Identify what users can reasonably verify and what responsibility remains with AI providers and deploying institutions.
